name: disktype
desc: Detect content format of a disk or disk image
why: Identifies filesystems, partition tables and content formats inside disk images, a satisfying way to see what is really on a disk.

brief.what_it_is: disktype is a command-line C program that inspects a disk or disk image and reports what content format it holds: file systems, partition tables, boot loaders, disk image wrappers, compression and archive formats. The input is a disk device or image file; the output is a textual description of the formats it recognizes. The homepage describes it as built to compile on any modern Unix flavour and self-contained, working without special libraries or headers.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says its purpose is 'to detect the content format of a disk or disk image'. It is aimed at finding out what is really on a disk, covering common file systems, partition tables and boot codes.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internal mechanism. It lists the formats it recognizes as of version 9, and says some system-dependent features can be used to gather additional information. Recognition appears to be signature-based, though the homepage does not say so directly.
brief.install_notes: No precompiled binaries are provided. Install by compiling the source tarball (disktype 9, 44K) from the homepage; the homepage calls this 'simple and straightforward'. Packages exist for Debian (maintained by Juan Manuel Garcia Molina, in unstable and testing), Fink (unstable tree), and Solaris via OpenCSW (maintained by Dagobert Michelsen). The homepage notes that it has been compiled on Linux, FreeBSD, NetBSD, Mac OS X/Darwin, BeOS, QNX, Solaris, HP/UX and Cygwin. Homebrew packaging is not mentioned on the homepage, so the brew install route was not verified from the source.
brief.standout: It recognizes a wide set of obscure formats (Amiga FFS/PFS/SFS, BeOS BFS, QNX4, 3DO CD-ROM, Xbox DVD, Sega Dreamcast boot, Atari ST AHDI3) alongside mainstream ones, and is self-contained with no libraries. The homepage points readers to gpart, file and GNU Parted as related tools for other jobs.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage shows version 9 as the latest release, with no release date given. It mentions a CVS repository and SourceForge trackers, but no recent activity is shown on the page. Documentation is described as 'still evolving'. The two documentation URLs I guessed returned 404, so I could not check the docs.
brief.caveats: No precompiled binaries are offered. The documentation is not bundled and the homepage says it is still evolving. The homepage lists some support as partial ('some variations' for UFS and SysV FS, 'limited' for Apple UDIF and Linux cloop). The homepage gives no licence. Build instructions beyond 'simple and straightforward' were not on the page I read.
quotes: The purpose of disktype is to detect the content format of a disk or disk image.
No precompiled binaries are available at this time. Compiling disktype is simple and straightforward, so I don't see this as a great loss.
It is self-contained and in general works without special libraries or headers.
